rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: HSE guidance covers infection risks in mortuaries, post-mortem rooms, funeral premises and exhumation work.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: HSE provides a dedicated COSHH control sheet for embalming with formaldehyde solutions.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: HSE directs post-mortem and embalming work to the specific guidance for managing infection risks when handling the deceased.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: Direct contact with blood or body fluids should be avoided where possible and restricted to workers trained to handle the material safely.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: Reusable equipment exposed to blood or body fluids can transmit infection if it is not adequately decontaminated.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: Formaldehyde can irritate the eyes, skin and respiratory tract.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: Prolonged formaldehyde exposure can contribute to skin sensitisation and allergic contact dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: Infection-control arrangements for funeral and mortuary work should reflect current scientific knowledge, work practices and the circumstances of handling human remains.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: Embalming risk depends on the condition of the deceased, procedure, formaldehyde concentration, ventilation, sharps, hygiene, PPE and worker competence.

rows.source: HSE embalming and deceased-person infection controls
rows.verified: Embalming evidence is chemical-, procedure-, infection-, facility- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Work-related contact dermatitis is identified as the most common occupational skin disease affecting dental teams.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Single-use medical gloves should be changed after every patient.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Dental gloves should fit correctly and be powder-free; latex gloves, where needed, should be low-protein and powder-free.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Hands should be washed after glove removal to remove chemical contamination.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Cool or tepid water, sparing use of hand-wash agents and thorough rinsing help reduce skin irritation.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Skin should be dried by patting with soft paper or cotton towels rather than rubbing.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Regular emollient use, particularly after clinical sessions, helps prevent excessive skin drying.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Dental procedures with potential blood transfer require risk assessment, safe systems of work and adequate decontamination practices.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Dental risk depends on glove material, wet-work frequency, cleaning chemicals, instruments, sharps, decontamination and individual skin condition.

rows.source: HSE dentistry skin and bloodborne-virus controls
rows.verified: Dentistry evidence is procedure-, instrument-, exposure-, patient- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level dermatitis or infection probability.
